title: Improved strategy for large scale isolation of sialylglycopeptide (SGP) from egg yolk powder
author: Alagesan, Kolarich

steps.title: Resuspend egg yolk powder
steps.instruction: Add 250 g of egg yolk powder to 750 mL Milli‑Q water (1:3 w/v) in a suitable vessel and stir at room temperature for 2 h (or overnight if preferred).

steps.title: Add methanol and stir
steps.instruction: Add 500 mL methanol (2 vol relative to the water) to the suspension, mix, and stir for an additional 1 h at room temperature.

steps.title: Aliquot and centrifuge first
steps.instruction: Dispense the mixture into 40 mL portions using 50 mL Falcon tubes, then centrifuge each tube at 3000 × g, 4 °C for 5 min.

steps.title: Add chloroform and centrifuge
steps.instruction: To each tube add 10 mL chloroform, mix thoroughly, and centrifuge again at 3000 × g, 4 °C for 10 min.

steps.title: Collect aqueous phase and concentrate
steps.instruction: Carefully decant the upper aqueous phase (which contains the sialylglycopeptide) from each tube, combine the pooled aqueous fractions, and remove solvent under reduced pressure with a rotary evaporator.

steps.title: Gel‑filtration purification
steps.instruction: Load the concentrated crude solution onto a Sephadex G‑50 (fine) column (25 × 935 mm), elute with 100 mM ammonium acetate (pH 7) at a flow rate of 1 mL min⁻¹ and 10 °C.

steps.title: Collect and pool positive fractions
steps.instruction: Collect sixty 10 mL fractions; test each for resorcinol positivity and pool all positive fractions together.

description: The ability to produce defined and well-characterised compounds by synthetic approaches has always been a major driving force in science. The establishment of synthetic routes allowing the production of defined DNA or peptide sequences in high yields and purity has been crucial for the development of biosciences and our current understanding of cellular functions [1,2]. However, to date the synthetic capacities to easily produce a large variety and quantity of synthetic glycopeptides is still lagging behind classical peptide or DNA synthesis strategies, also because of the large structure complexity associated with glycans. Despite tremendous advances in carbohydrate chemistry [[3], [4], [5]] the production of large oligosaccharides with diverse building blocks still requires substantial time and material resources. In particular, introduction of certain biologically important glyco-features such as α-fucose, α-sialyl or β-mannose linkages between the monosaccharide building blocks are challenging and represent major limiting steps in the production of sufficient quantities of larger oligosaccharides such as N-glycans. Despite these challenges, total complete synthesis of glycopeptide bearing fucosylated biantennary, disialylated N-glycans was in principle accomplished by the Danishefsky research group [6], though with considerable efforts that yet make it unfeasible for routine production. One way of circumventing these obstacles is to make use of nature's glycosylation potential by isolating the compounds of interest from natural resources such as egg yolk [[7], [8], [9], [10], [11]]. These compounds can easily be purified and subsequently transformed into protected building blocks, which then can be used for glycoconjugate synthesis [[7], [8], [9], [10], [11]]. This approach is significantly more cost effective, quicker and allows the production of g-quantities within just 2–3 weeks.
